newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Hashimoto assures China on islands, war record.
newsitem.headline: Hashimoto assures China on islands, war record.

text.p: Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto reassured China on Sunday over an island dispute which has soured relations and reiterated an apology over Japan's World War Two aggression, Japanese officials said.

He referred to the dispute over the Diaoyu islands -- known as the Senkakus in Japan -- during a meeting with Chinese President Jiang Zemin on the sidelines of an annual conference of Asia-Pacific leaders on Monday.
Japanese rightists caused an uproar by erecting a beacon on one of the small rocky East China Sea islands as a sign of Japan's claims of sovereignty, disputed by China and Taiwan.

"We do not want a repeat of the events of July (on the islands) that could damage Sino-Japanese ties and we are ready to make efforts towards that end," a senior Japanese official who attended the talks quoted Hashimoto as saying.

Sino-Japanese ties plummetted this year over the islands dispute and a visit by Hashimoto to Tokyo's Yasukuni Shrine, which is dedicated to Japan's 2.6 million war dead since the 19th century, including war criminals like General Hideki Tojo.
Hashimoto and Jiang will meet again at the summit of leaders of the 18-member Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum at Subic Bay, a former U.S. navy base northwest of Manila.
Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman Shen Guofang said in a separate briefing that Jiang warned Hashimoto against any resurgence of militarism in Japan and any further trouble in the islands dispute.
He also quoted Jiang as saying Japanese government leaders should refrain from visiting the Yasukuni Shrine. Hashimoto's visit in July was the first by a Japanese prime minister in 10 years.
Hashimoto was quoted by the Japanese official as saying Japan would not return to militarism.
"Our government inherits the war apology issued by the previous prime minister in 1995...There are no moves to bring back militarism," Hashimoto said.
The Japanese prime minister verbally repeated a 1995 government apology for the "great damage and pain" inflicted on neighbours including China during World War Two.
It was unusual for a prime minister to repeat the statement, but Hashimoto apparently did so to prove his sincerity, Japanese sources said.
Hashimoto also assured Jiang that Japan's moves to strengthen security ties with the United States were not directed at any other country and that Japan did not support the independence of Taiwan.
"We only ask for a peaceful solution to the China-Taiwan problem through dialogue," Hashimoto told Jiang.
The Chinese spokesman said Jiang had "expressed his appreciation for the positions indicated by Prime Minister Hashimoto".
Shen said Hashimoto had invited Jiang to pay a state visit to Japan next year, the 25th anniversary of the resumption of diplomatic relations between the two states.

The Japanese official said Jiang also thanked Hashimoto for Japan's continued support for China's bid to join the World Trade Organisation (WTO), which regulates international trade, and for re-starting work on a $5.3 billion yen-loan package for China for 1996-1999.
But there was no word on lifting Japan's frozen grant-in-aid for China, worth $63 million.
The grant, a fraction of the larger yen loan package, was frozen as a sanction against China's nuclear tests this year, the first time Japan had used aid as a political weapon against China.
